aboutPage.tagline: A student-led advocacy initiative at Metro Academic & Classical High School.
aboutPage.missionBody:
This website is the culmination of our Advocacy Project for Mr. Boyle’s class. Our goal is to address the critical breakdown of the recycling infrastructure in St. Louis. By synthesizing academic research, city policy, and direct interviews, we aim to provide a clear roadmap for residents to navigate the current 'Drop-Off' model.

As per the project requirements, we have curated 15 high-quality academic sources and conducted a primary interview with a city authority to ensure our information is both accurate and actionable.
aboutPage.contextQuote: "Explore and research a cause you care deeply about, find an authority figure to interview, and raise awareness for the issue by publishing research in a meaningful way."

article.title: The Curbside Crisis
article.body: Due to labor shortages and high contamination rates, St. Louis has officially pivoted to a 'Drop-Off' model. Placing recyclables in your alley bin now almost guarantees they end up in a landfill.

additionalArticles.title: What Can Actually Be Recycled?
additionalArticles.body: It's essential to only drop off the 'Core Four': Clean paper/cardboard, plastic bottles/jugs with caps, glass bottles/jars, and metal cans. When in doubt, throw it out.

contentBlocks.body: We talk to the mayor to learn more

contentBlocks.label: New Update
contentBlocks.title: Recycling, the Transition
contentBlocks.body: St. Louis is in a weird spot right now
contentBlocks.expandableBody: St. Louis is in a weird spot with its trash and recycling right now. Most people have noticed that we aren’t really using the old alleyway recycling system anymore. The city basically had to switch things up because the alley bins were getting way too much contamination. It’s actually really expensive; we spend a lot more trying to process messy recycling than we do just hauling away regular trash. If you want to make sure your stuff actually gets recycled, the "St. Louis City Recycles" site says you have to follow the rules, like never putting your items in plastic bags (Saint Louis City Recycles, 2026). They also have specific pickup days now, usually Monday and Friday or Tuesday and Thursday, depending on where you live (Saint Louis City Recycles, 2026). Local officials have said that this "recycling revamp is already paying off," but it really comes down to us (Krull, 2025). If citizens don’t do their part to sort things right, the whole system is basically "impossible" to pull off on a mass scale (Echeverría et al., 2020). Research suggests that "formal recycling" done by organized enterprises is much more efficient than informal or uncoordinated efforts (Burcea, 2015). It is also important to recognize that a "quiet revolution" is happening in sorting technology, which might eventually help the city manage waste more effectively (Carey, 2017). Ultimately, the system is "impossible" to pull off on a mass scale without citizens doing their part to keep the stream clean. As the city looks toward the future, the goal is to close the gap between what we spend on waste versus what we can recover through a functional, citizen-supported system.

contentBlocks.label: Insider Info
contentBlocks.title: Closed and Open Circular Economies
contentBlocks.body: Learn how recycling helps the economy
contentBlocks.expandableBody: Recycling isn't just a chore; it’s a vital part of a much larger system known as the Circular Economy. The general idea is that resources should be used repeatedly—essentially "reusing items instead of discarding them after a single use"—until they literally cannot be used anymore (Akenji et al., 2019). The ultimate goal is to "decrease the material disposed of, and the new products created" (U.S. EPA, 2025). Nationally, the EPA is pushing this through a "National recycling goal" to increase recycling rates by 50% (U.S. EPA, 2026). This is supported by the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act, a law passed by Congress to spark innovation and fund groups that help keep our oceans and environments clean (U.S. Congress, 2020). However, we have to be realistic because recycling is "never perfect" (van Ewijk & Stegemann, 2023). There is a big difference between closed-loop recycling, where a product (like a glass bottle) is turned back into the exact same thing, and open-loop or "down-cycling" (van Ewijk & Stegemann, 2023). In down-cycling, materials lose quality each time they are processed, eventually becoming "lesser products" that can't be reused again (Jain, 2021). This is a major challenge for plastics, which are made of complex polymers and "additives" like glass fiber that can make up 5% to 80% of the material (Goodship, 2007). Despite these challenges, there are some really interesting things happening right here in Missouri. The Department of Natural Resources recently funded a "study on the ability to use recycled tires in concrete" (Missouri Department of Natural Resources, 2020). The study found that using old tires actually makes concrete better at blocking out noise while allowing us to use less raw limestone. By focusing on these kinds of innovative, state-specific solutions, we can work toward a future where "innovation" and "incentives" finally help us tackle the piles of plastic waste we produce (Carey, 2017).

contentBlocks.label: National Strategy
contentBlocks.title: Building a Better Recycling System
contentBlocks.body: It is important to build towards a recycling system that will bring on a new age in Saint Louis.
contentBlocks.expandableBody: It is important to build towards a recycling system that will bring on a new age in Saint Louis. One proposed nation-wide solution to recycling is the "National Recycling Strategy," which focuses on improving the markets surrounding recycling commodities, improving infrastructure, reducing non-recyclables entering the recycling process, increasing pro-recycling policies, and making a standard data collection system. The "National Recycling Strategy" was proposed by (EPA, 2026). If more people recycled, then our nation and city would be better off, but why is this, and what is recycling? "Recycling, also called material recovery, is the use of waste to make new materials and products" (Ewijk, Stijn van, and Julia Stegemann., 2023). It is important for people to recycle because it powers the circular economy. A circular economy is an economy where goods are put into a cycle, they start their journey as one thing and get reused and recycled repeatedly until they are no longer reusable (Akenji et al., 2019). This same article also discusses how circular economies breed innovation and economic growth. It is important for expanding the circular economy to tell others to recycle, but you should also tell them what can and cannot be recycled. Only plastics with the RIC codes 1 and 2 can be legitimately recycled (Jain, Akshat, editor., 2026). It’s important to look online to see if your items can or cannot be recycled, especially before bringing them to the recycling plants, as non-recyclables jam systems and cost cities hundreds of thousands. Nearly $630,000 could be saved yearly on recycling if our practices changed and less trash was in the recycling stream (City of Saint Louis Missouri, 2026). The major issue wasting the city’s money is non-recyclables ending up in recycling bins. Large costs are one of the major factors that led to the city stopping the alley recycling program. The "National Recycling Strategy" may be a long term and large-scale solution, but if you, personally, would like to make a difference concerning recycling, prove it. You can prove your dedication to recycling by sorting out recyclables and non-recyclables to prevent unneeded block ups that waste public tax dollars. Everyone should recycle, it will prove to the government that this is an issue we care about, don’t just vote with a ballot, vote with you actions, show that recycling is a cause you care about, go to a local recycling center, tell others about the importance of recycling, make your voice and your opinions heard.

contentBlocks.label: Recycling Challenges
contentBlocks.title: The Difficulties of Recycling
contentBlocks.body: What are the difficulties associated with recycling, and how might this relate to the climate surrounding recycling in Saint Louis?
contentBlocks.expandableBody: What are the difficulties associated with recycling, and how might this relate to the change climate surrounding recycling in Saint Louis? The biggest issue with recycling is that only some materials can be recycled. Often times, only RIC system codes 1 and 2 can be recycled in mass amounts (Jain, Akshat, editor, 2026). In addition to constraints in what plastics can be recycled, plastic’s biggest draw for consumers is also a large drawback. Plastics are often praised for being so durable, but this also makes them more difficult to break down by the environment, which can lead to blockages in sewage systems, habitat destruction, and these plastics can even end up building up in the bodies of humans and animals (Akenji, Lewis, et al, 2026). One major restraint we currently have in the recycling sector is the lack of appropriate equipment for recycling metals. Metal recycling often requires extracting small bits of metal out of complicated items like computers. Two solution that should majorly improve recycling of metals are, A, improved product designs that allow for easier extraction of valuable metals, and B, better technologies for extracting the metals (van Ewijk, Stijn, and Julia Stegemann, 2023). Recycling imposes many difficulties that derive from the technologies we use for recycling materials and how they have not been keeping up with the world’s ever-changing streams of waste. The "National Recycling Strategy," which would create standardized goals nation wide for recycling. The general goal for the "National Recycling Strategy" is to advance nation wide recycling technologies and to reach a recycling rate of 50% by 2030. (EPA, 2026)

contentBlocks.label: Take Action
contentBlocks.title: What You Can Do Now
contentBlocks.body: What can you personally do in this uncertain time to keep recycling?
contentBlocks.expandableBody: What can you personally do in this uncertain time? The city outlines a straightforward way to keep recycling even when the convenience of alley dumpsters is no longer available. In areas where roll-carts are not available, the city recommends setting recycling aside so you can bring it to one of the 46 drop off locations located in the city (STLCityRecyclables, 2026). For easy access to these locations, you can click the "map" section on the top of our website. The city has claimed they’ve already started seeing savings from ending the alley recycling program, they claim saving "$100,000 over 30 days," while still recycling a 80% of the amount they did with alley dumpsters (STL Mag, 2026). Hopefully the city can use these savings to build out new infrastructure for recycling. Although it is frustrating that recycling is experiencing major reforms in Saint Louis, it is important to understand why the city has taken the actions it has. We want you to go out to your local recycling drop-off centers to recycle your waste materials, while being mindful of what you drop-off, making sure you do not to leave materials that may be difficult for waste management centers.
